flags.current: *(Note the ILM formula discrepancy flagged in the front matter of this curriculum: use the plain-ratio form, $\text{ILM} = \ln[\exp(1) - 1 + (LC / BIC)]$, rather than the exponentiated form that appears in a footnote elsewhere; no question in this document requires the ILM to be computed.)*
flags.proposed: *(Formula reference: the finalised December 2017 standard sets $\text{ILM} = \ln\left[\exp(1) - 1 + \left(\tfrac{LC}{BIC}\right)^{0.8}\right]$, with $LC = 15 \times$ average annual operational risk losses over the previous ten years. The plain-ratio form without the 0.8 exponent comes from the March 2016 consultative document. No question in this set requires the ILM to be computed.)*
flags.source_says: Front matter (PDF p.2): 'Chapter 2 and Chapter 24 both state ILM = Ln[exp(1) - 1 + (LC/BIC)] whereas footnote 5 of the high-level summary in Chapter 25 states ... (LC/BIC)^0.8 ... The exponent appeared in the Committee's consultative work and the plain ratio in the finalised standard ... Use the plain ratio'. Q33 trap line (PDF p.28): 'Note the ILM formula discrepancy flagged in the front matter: use the plain ratio.'
flags.derivation: The source has the history the wrong way round. BCBS d424 (Basel III: Finalising post-crisis reforms, Dec 2017, operational risk section; now OPE25) defines ILM = ln(exp(1) - 1 + (LC/BIC)^0.8). The plain ratio ln(e - 1 + LC/BIC) was the March 2016 SMA consultative form (d355). The curriculum notes for Ch 24 (notes/FRM_Consolidated_Vol1/ch/12_OR_ORR24.tex lines 70-75) also give the ^0.8 form, which contradicts the source's claim that Ch 24 states the plain ratio. Numerically, with LC/BIC = 1.1236: plain ILM = 1.0445, exponent ILM = 1.0353, so the two forms give different answers. The JSON goes further than the source by printing the plain-ratio formula outright and telling the candidate to prefer it. The answer key (a) is not affected. Note: other OR.json items outside this slice (around lines 3602, 3783 and 3905 of content/OR.json) also use the plain form, so they should be checked against the ^0.8 form.
flags.evidence: PDF p.2 front matter 'GROUND-TRUTH CONFLICT INSIDE THE CURRICULUM, FLAGGED'; PDF pp.27-28 Q33 trap note; notes 12_OR_ORR24.tex L70-75 '\ln[e^1-1+(loss component/BIC)^{0.8}]'

flags.current: In the cloud provider breach, the intrusion originated with a contractor at the provider exploiting the provider's own misconfigured firewall, and the bank was still ultimately responsible.
flags.proposed: In the cloud provider breach (Capital One on AWS), a former employee of the cloud provider exploited a misconfigured firewall to reach unencrypted customer data. Both firms knew of the vulnerability, and the bank was still held ultimately responsible and fined USD 80 million for inadequate risk management of its cloud provider.
flags.source_says: Same wording as the JSON (PDF p.13 Q14 solution): 'the intrusion originated with a contractor at the provider exploiting the provider's own misconfigured firewall'.
flags.derivation: Case recall is what LO6 tests. The curriculum (notes 19_OR_ORR13.tex L66-83) says a former AWS employee exploited a weakness in the cloud-storage firewall; both Capital One and AWS were aware of the vulnerability; the data was unencrypted; and Capital One was fined USD 80m for failing to assess and manage its AWS risk. The attacker was a former employee, not a contractor. In the actual event, the misconfigured web application firewall was Capital One's own configuration, not 'the provider's own' firewall. The answer key (a) is unaffected, but the recalled fact is wrong and could be tested directly.
flags.evidence: PDF p.13 (Q14 solution); notes FRM_Consolidated_Vol1/ch/19_OR_ORR13.tex L62-85

flags.current: The clearest illustration in the curriculum is the payment protection insurance episode, where the Lloyds Banking Group paid GBP 21.9 billion, roughly USD 28 billion, in regulatory fines and customer compensation over 2015 to 2019 for failing to handle claims fairly and for misinforming customers when selling insurance alongside banking products.
flags.proposed: Replace with the Ch 14 case set: 'The curriculum's cases are UBS (2008, misrepresenting risky securities as safe; the largest penalty by far), JPMorgan (2020, USD 920 million for spoofing, a market-manipulation case) and Deutsche Bank (2022, USD 2 million for best-execution failures). The lesson is that misrepresentation to clients draws the heaviest sanctions, while even technical breaches such as order execution are penalised.' If the PPI example is kept, present it as a general illustration, not as a curriculum case, and drop the '2015 to 2019' period, since Lloyds' PPI redress ran from 2011.
flags.source_says: Same wording as the JSON (PDF p.15 Q16 solution).
flags.derivation: In the curriculum notes (35_OR_ORR14.tex, LO 53b), the Ch 14 investor-protection case studies are UBS 2008 (selling risky securities as safe), JPMorgan 2020 spoofing (USD 920m) and Deutsche Bank 2022 best execution (USD 2m). The OR notes never mention Lloyds or PPI. Calling PPI 'the clearest illustration in the curriculum' misattributes the case, and it hides that two of the three actual cases are not mis-selling. Option (a) is still the best of the four, so the key stands. Low confidence because the notes are a summary of the GARP chapter.
flags.evidence: PDF p.15 Q16 solution; notes FRM_Consolidated_Vol1/ch/35_OR_ORR14.tex L60-80
